covers.quote: Legal documents and many specialist and professional publications use specific contractions.
Avoid using contractions of single words in more formal content such as high-level briefing and responses to official inquiries.
The exceptions are contractions used in formal writing, such as ‘Dr’ and other titles.
Grammatical contractions are not generally used in formal content.
You can use them in less formal content which aims to create:
a conversational tone (for example, in a newsletter)
a friendly or collaborative tone (for example, in brochures and manuals).

examples.note: Presented as formal content.

parts.quote: The department has not breached its staffing cap.

examples.note: Presented as less formal content.

parts.quote: The department hasn’t breached its staffing cap.

examples.note: Presented as friendly and conversational content.

parts.quote: We appreciate that the new rules weren’t advertised widely. We’re now contacting everyone who might be affected. Please don’t hesitate to contact us if you have any questions.

rules.specification: Assess formality from the document's purpose and context. High-level briefings and responses to official inquiries are explicit formal cases. The page does not provide an exhaustive list of contractions accepted in formal writing.
rules.violation_condition: Formal content contains contractions other than established contractions accepted in formal writing.
when: Applies to both single-word and grammatical contractions in formal content.
Contractions conventionally used in formal writing, such as ‘Dr’ and other titles, are exceptions.
Legal documents and specialist and professional publications use specific contractions.
Grammatical contractions are permitted in less formal content intended to create a conversational, friendly or collaborative tone.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 combine the formal-content restriction and its restatements; G-3 records accepted formal forms and informal uses as exceptions rather than separate rules.

covers.quote: Don’t place a full stop after contractions.
The exception is when the contraction ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark.

examples.note: No full stop after the contraction.

parts.quote: Tempo Australia Ltd hired him last year.

examples.note: The full stop ends the sentence.

parts.quote: He is currently working for Tempo Australia Ltd.

examples.note: Another punctuation mark ends the sentence.

parts.quote: They said they can’t!

rules.quote: Don’t end contractions with full stops
rules.violation_condition: A contraction is followed by a full stop that is not needed to end its sentence, including an additional full stop when another punctuation mark ends the sentence.
when: A full stop is permitted when the contraction ends a sentence and is not followed by another punctuation mark.
rules.why: G-4 treats the body instruction as a restatement; G-2 and G-3 retain sentence-ending punctuation as a condition on the same check.

rules.quote: Don’t use an apostrophe to show missing letters in a contraction of a single word (‘Dr’, ‘Ltd’).
rules.violation_condition: A single-word contraction contains an apostrophe marking omitted letters.
when: Applies to contractions of single words, not grammatical contractions joining two words.
Concerns apostrophes marking omitted letters, not apostrophes serving another grammatical function.
rules.why: The single-word prohibition is a distinct check from the apostrophe-count rule for grammatical contractions.

examples.note: The manual labels this Correct.

parts.quote: shan’t

examples.note: The manual labels this Incorrect.

parts.quote: sha’n’t

rules.quote: Grammatical contractions use only one apostrophe, even if the contraction leaves out letters from more than one place.
rules.violation_condition: A grammatical contraction contains more than one apostrophe to mark omitted letters.
when: Applies to grammatical contractions joining two words.
Omission of letters from multiple places does not justify additional apostrophes.
rules.why: G-2 keeps multiple omission sites within one apostrophe-count check; E-2 attaches the Correct/Incorrect pair to this nearest rule.

covers.quote: Use the capitalisation that you would use for the uncontracted word.
Capitalisation of the uncontracted word depends on the context.

examples.note: The contraction is part of the event name.

parts.quote: The Cth Games

examples.note: The contraction is generic.

parts.quote: A cth is a term for a political community.

rules.quote: Capitalise contractions in the same way as the full word
rules.violation_condition: A contraction has capitalisation different from that required for its uncontracted form in the same context.
when: Determine the capitalisation of the full word in its actual context, including whether it is part of a name or is generic.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the heading and body restatement; E-1 keeps both contextual capitalisation examples compliant.

covers.quote: Write out the contracted term in full unless it’s a grammatical contraction.

examples.note: The initial word is written in full.

parts.quote: Commonwealth resources are available.

examples.note: The initial contraction is grammatical.

parts.quote: Don’t forget your notes for the meeting.

rules.quote: Use the full word at start of the sentence (except for grammatical contractions)
rules.violation_condition: A sentence begins with a contracted term that is not a grammatical contraction.
when: Applies at the start of a sentence.
Grammatical contractions may start a sentence.
rules.why: G-4 keeps the body restatement with its heading, which supplies the sentence-start scope; G-3 treats grammatical contractions as an exception.

covers.quote: Only use the contraction ‘no’ when immediately followed by a numeral.
In all other instances, write the word out in full so it isn’t confused with the negation ‘no’.

examples.note: The contraction immediately precedes a numeral.

parts.quote: Archive box no 152 has been found in the basement.

examples.note: The word is written in full.

parts.quote: I won’t be able to get their manager’s number until tomorrow.

examples.note: The word is written in full.

parts.quote: There are a number of options available to us.

examples.note: The manual labels this Not this.

parts.quote: I won’t be able to get their manager’s no until tomorrow.

examples.note: The manual labels this Not this.

parts.quote: There are a no of options available to us.

rules.quote: Only use the contraction ‘no’ with numerals
rules.violation_condition: The contraction ‘no’ meaning ‘number’ is not immediately followed by a numeral.
when: Applies to ‘no’ used as a contraction meaning ‘number’, not to the negation ‘no’.
The numeral must immediately follow the contraction.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 combine the numeral restriction and its complementary full-word instruction into one check.
